teaching.causalExplanation: About thirteen point eight billion years ago, the Universe was extremely hot and dense, and it's been expanding ever since. That's the Big Bang model. It isn't an explosion into empty space. Space itself is stretching, everywhere at once, so there's no centre. As space stretches, so does every light wave travelling through it. A longer wavelength means less energy per photon, because E equals h c over lambda. And by Wien's law, the peak wavelength is b over T. So double the size of the Universe, and the temperature halves. Here's the rule that turns light into matter. Two photons meeting head-on with equal energies can make a particle and its antiparticle, but only if each photon brings at least the particle's rest energy, m c squared. When the Universe was very hot, most photons had far more than that, so pairs formed and annihilated all the time, in balance. As it cooled, typical photons fell below the threshold. Only the rare, extra energetic photons could still make pairs, while annihilation carried on. Cooling starves the making. So how hot for electrons? The electron's rest energy, m c squared, is eight point two times ten to the minus fourteen joules. A photon with that energy has a wavelength of h c over E, two point four times ten to the minus twelve metres. Now use Wien's law backwards. T equals b over lambda, which gives about one point two times ten to the nine kelvin. It's an estimate, but it gives the scale, about a billion kelvin, which the Universe cooled through in its first few minutes.

**Boundary:** starts on m7-v16's final frame (pair production in a cooling hot early Universe, with the grey tag "head-on, equal energies"). Teaches: the hot Big Bang model as expansion of space with no centre; expansion stretches wavelengths, so photon energy and temperature fall (Wien's law, size doubles, temperature halves); the threshold rule for pair production (two photons meeting head-on with equal energies: each needs at least mc²); a Wien estimate of the temperature scale for electron pairs (about 10⁹ K); heavier particles first (protons at about 2 × 10¹² K); quarks to protons and neutrons at about a millionth of a second; the tiny matter excess (more than a billion photons per proton or neutron); why neutrons became scarce (heavier, and free neutrons decay, half-life about 10 minutes; about 1 neutron per 7 protons); the deuterium wait until about 10⁹ K and 3 minutes; the 25% helium count; nuclei but not atoms (free electrons, opaque plasma); recombination at about 380 000 years and 3000 K; transparency; first stars after a few hundred million years. Stops before the evidence (redshift, Hubble's law, the CMB as an observation, abundances as a test: v02), Planck time and inflation (site "beyond the syllabus"), and quantitative T ∝ 1/a calculations.

## Decisions

- **Learner question (route wording kept).** "How did cooling radiation allow matter to form in the early Universe?" The answer is one rule used twice: cooling first makes particle-pair making rare while annihilation continues, leaving a small excess of matter (3 to 6); then cooling stops photons breaking the structures matter forms, first nuclei (8, 9), much later atoms (10, 11).
- **Hook (from m7-v16's final frame; site predict "What would happen to the temperature of the universe as it shrinks?" reversed).** 3 s prediction chips: "more pairs", "fewer pairs", "no change". Answer: fewer pairs, because fewer photons reach the threshold.
- **Expansion, not explosion (site `trace-the-model-timeline`: "expansion of space itself ... not an explosion into pre-existing space").** A coded square grid of dots stretches uniformly; every dot sees the others recede; a dashed "centre?" ring is crossed. The site's balloon analogy is replaced by a flat grid (the balloon's surface invites "the centre is inside the balloon"; author note a).
- **Cooling mechanism (site "Understand: Universe cooled as it expanded: T ∝ 1/a").** Taught causally with Module 7 tools: stretched wavelength, E = hc/λ, λ_max = b/T. Stated in words ("double the size, the temperature halves"); T ∝ 1/a is not written (site marks quantitative scale-factor work as extension).
- **Threshold rule (recalled from m7-v16's handoff; Revision 2).** In the drawn case, two photons meeting head-on with equal energies, pair production needs each photon to bring at least mc² of the particle; annihilation needs no threshold. Hot: making and annihilating in balance. Cool: typical photons fall below the threshold, so making becomes rare (only the energetic tail can still do it) while annihilation carries on, and the pairs die away. The narration says "meeting head-on" in scenes 1 and 3 ("with equal energies" in 3), the chip carries it, and A1's card says it; author note (h) gives the general condition. The same energetic tail is what breaks deuterium in scene 8, so the two scenes tell one consistent story.
- **Worked estimate (new, original).** The temperature at which a photon at the Wien peak carries m_ec²: E = 8.2 × 10⁻¹⁴ J, λ = hc/E = 2.4 × 10⁻¹² m, T = b/λ = 1.2 × 10⁹ K. Narrated and tagged as an estimate of the scale (author note b explains why the real pair era spans several billion kelvin down to about 10⁹ K, seconds to minutes). Three stages, one at a time, givens grouped with units.
- **Heavier particles first.** Proton rest energy about 1836 times the electron's (data-sheet masses: 940 MeV), so its Wien scale is about 2 × 10¹² K; quarks bind into protons and neutrons at about a millionth of a second (site timeline "t ≈ 10⁻⁶ s: Quarks combine to form protons and neutrons").
- **Matter excess (site "Formation of fundamental particles").** One sentence on the unexplained asymmetry; "about one extra particle for every billion pairs"; photons outnumber protons and neutrons "more than a billion to one" (Planck 2018 baryon-to-photon ratio η = 6.1 × 10⁻¹⁰, about 1.6 × 10⁹ photons per baryon; author note c). Neutrinos are not mentioned (author note d).
- **Neutron scarcity (new causal step, needed for the helium count).** The neutron is slightly heavier (1.29 MeV; data-sheet masses give 1.1 MeV, not shown), and free neutrons decay with a half-life of about 10 minutes. Result stated: about 1 neutron per 7 protons when fusion began (author note e).
- **Deuterium wait (site Activity 1 Q2 asks the parallel question for the CMB).** Deuterium binding 2.2 MeV; more than a billion photons per nucleon means the energetic tail of the photon spectrum breaks deuterium until about 10⁹ K, about 3 minutes (site "t ≈ 3 min: Nucleosynthesis").
- **25% helium (new, original count).** 2 neutrons + 14 protons → one ⁴He + 12 ¹H: helium is 4 of 16 mass units, 25%; hydrogen 75%; traces of deuterium, helium-3, lithium (site lesson 2 figure; lesson 7 "~75% by mass", "~25%"). Fusion ends after about 20 minutes (site lesson 2 Figure 2 "~20 min nucleosynthesis ends"; site note 1 on lesson 7's "3 minutes"). The observed abundance is not stated here; v02 tests it.
- **Nuclei against atoms (route stop "distinguish nuclei from neutral atoms"; site "Account 6 marks").** Hydrogen's 13.6 eV against deuterium's 2.2 MeV (about 1.6 × 10⁵ times larger); free electrons scatter photons, so the plasma is opaque ("glowing fog"). Recombination at about 380 000 years and about 3000 K (site), Universe transparent. The CMB is named only in the handoff as "that light" (v02 owns it).
- **Timeline (site Activity 1 events; inflation omitted as extension).** Log-time axis with a falling temperature bar; first stars "a few hundred million years later" (site "~200 million years"; author note f).
- **Memory aid (scene 12, new): "Too cool to make pairs, then too cool to break nuclei, then too cool to break atoms."** See "Memory aid check".
- **Attempts (original, HSC style).** A1 (3 marks): the Wien estimate for muon pairs (muon mass given; students met muons in m7-v13): E = 1.69 × 10⁻¹¹ J; λ = 1.18 × 10⁻¹⁴ m; T = 2.5 × 10¹¹ K. This section tops the design up to the checklist used for Year 11 Physics, Biology and Chemistry, and applies root rules R1 to R4 (`../checks/root-acceptance-y11-upgrade-12-nov.md`). Where a scene has an "Upgrade (Revision 3)" paragraph, it adds to the Visual and wins wherever the two differ. No narration line changed.

- **Board stages.** (A) the last frame of Module 7, then the photon field with the painted galaxy, scene 1 (about 32 s); (B) the expanding grid, scene 2 (about 40 s); (C) the threshold gauge, scene 3 (about 39 s); (D) the working layout, scene 4 (about 36 s); (E) the two-threshold gauge with the temperature bar, scene 5 (about 28 s); (F) the field of protons and antiprotons, scene 6 (about 30 s); (G) the particle tally and the two mass bars, scene 7 (about 29 s); (H) the nucleus builder, scene 8 (about 27 s); (I) the sixteen discs, scene 9 (about 33 s); (J) the field of nuclei, electrons and photons: nuclei, then atoms, scenes 10 and 11 (about 60 s; the temperature bar reaches 3000 K at about 30 s); (K) the timeline with the live cooling dial and the memory card, scene 12 (about 23 s); question and feedback cards; the handoff; the notes board. No set-up runs past about 60 s, so no cut was needed.
- **Simulation engines (`src/explainer/sims/`).** Three fields run on the particle box engine (`particle-box.ts`, drawn with `ParticleBoxView`, counts with `countAt`). Scene 6: protons and antiprotons as two species with a two-particle reaction that removes a pair, so the discs thin out and a few protons are left over; the starting counts are a model (for example 31 against 30) and the tag says "model: the real excess was about one in a billion". Scene 8: a proton and a neutron join, and a one-particle reaction with an activation energy breaks the pair again; a falling `temperature` timeline lets deuterium survive only once it is cool enough. Scenes 10 and 11 use the same pattern for electrons joining nuclei, with the free electron count falling as the temperature bar reaches about 3000 K. The cooling dial in scene 12 and the threshold gauges are exact arithmetic (Wien's law and E = mc²), lesson-coded.
- **Answer frames and mistakes (root rule R1).** Every answer sits in a dark-ink frame with an ink tick. Every mistake takes a slate scribble and a slate hand tag; "not possible" takes a slate cross. This overrides any red crossing, strike, chip or tag in the Visual lines and in "Colour roles". Red and green keep only their subject meanings.
- **Solid ink (root rule R2).** The opening frame and the final frame are drawn solid in full ink wherever a line calls part of them "faint", "ghost", "pale", "dim" or "grey", so both sides of each join match. Text a student must read is never faint: an earlier row that "dims" stays solid at a smaller size, and an earlier path that "stays faint" is a thin solid line in its role colour.
- **No coded drawings of real objects.** Apparatus and real objects are painted plates (the `y12p-` set or existing plates), scaled uniformly and never stretched. Exam-style outlines (ground, walls, cliffs, bench edges), vectors, field lines, graphs and circuit symbols stay coded, as root decision 3 for this course records.
- **No video numbers on screen.** Where a Visual line tags something with a video code, the on-screen words say "last time", "an earlier video" or "next time". Video codes in this document are notes for the builder.
- **Question cards.** Each attempt card arrives whole (sentences 38 px) with a picture from its first frame. The picture is answer-free: nothing on it can be counted, measured or read off to get the answer. Method aids (ledgers, formula strips, memory cards) are hidden while a countdown runs; every supplied value and condition stays on the card. Each feedback scene keeps a navy givens strip from its first frame.
- **Notes scene.** Five one-line bullets (95 characters or fewer, 34 px, role colours), the framed memory card beside them, and a notes scene of 45 s in all.

scenes.teachingReason: About thirteen point eight billion years ago, the Universe was extremely hot and dense, and it's been expanding ever since. That's the Big Bang model. It isn't an explosion into empty space. Space itself is stretching, everywhere at once, so there's no centre. As space stretches, so does every light wave travelling through it. A longer wavelength means less energy per photon, because E equals h c over lambda. And by Wien's law, the peak wavelength is b over T. So double the size of the Universe, and the temperature halves.

scenes.teachingReason: Here's the rule that turns light into matter. Two photons meeting head-on with equal energies can make a particle and its antiparticle, but only if each photon brings at least the particle's rest energy, m c squared. When the Universe was very hot, most photons had far more than that, so pairs formed and annihilated all the time, in balance. As it cooled, typical photons fell below the threshold. Only the rare, extra energetic photons could still make pairs, while annihilation carried on. Cooling starves the making.

scenes.teachingReason: So how hot for electrons? The electron's rest energy, m c squared, is eight point two times ten to the minus fourteen joules. A photon with that energy has a wavelength of h c over E, two point four times ten to the minus twelve metres. Now use Wien's law backwards. T equals b over lambda, which gives about one point two times ten to the nine kelvin. It's an estimate, but it gives the scale, about a billion kelvin, which the Universe cooled through in its first few minutes.

scenes.teachingReason: If matter and antimatter came in equal pairs, why didn't they annihilate completely? They almost did. For reasons physicists are still investigating, there was a tiny excess of matter, about one extra particle per billion pairs. That excess survived, outnumbered by photons more than a billion to one. Electrons and positrons did the same a few seconds later, leaving the electrons we're made of.

With the free electrons gone, light stopped scattering and travelled straight across space. The Universe became transparent.
